planting.note: Plant pre-soaked corms in fall for winter and spring bloom, claw-side down, 2 inches deep. Bloomingdale is a dwarf, early-flowering F1 series bred for pots, window boxes, and small-space bedding, reaching flower well ahead of taller garden strains.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil, soaking corms for a few hours before planting to rehydrate them. Bloomingdale is a compact, dwarf ranunculus series bred for container and bedding use, staying noticeably shorter and earlier-flowering than tall cut-flower strains while still producing the same densely layered, rose-like double blooms across a broad color range. Its low, tidy habit suits window boxes, mixed pots, and the front of a bed where taller ranunculus would need staking or crowd neighboring plants. As with other ranunculus, the corms decline once summer heat arrives, so lift and store them dry or treat plantings as an annual in most climates.

planting.note: Plant pre-soaked corms in fall for winter and spring bloom, claw-side down, 2 inches deep. Success is a vigorous, tall-growing ranunculus series bred for commercial cut-flower production, valued for its long stems and large, fully double blooms.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; good drainage is essential since ranunculus corms rot readily in wet winter soil. Success is a tall, vigorous ranunculus series grown primarily for cut-flower production, producing long, sturdy stems topped with large, tightly layered double blooms across a wide color range, making it a favorite among growers who need stems long enough for tall vases and mixed bouquets. Its taller habit means it benefits from some support or planting among companions that offer wind protection in open beds. Dig and store corms after foliage yellows in regions where summer heat and humidity would otherwise rot them in the ground.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Gainsborough is a long-grown, tall-spiked hybrid mullein prized for its soft, primrose-yellow flowers.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; heavy or poorly drained soil quickly rots the roots of this hybrid mullein. Gainsborough sends up tall, branching spires clothed in soft, pale primrose-yellow flowers over gray-green, felted foliage, a gentler and more refined color than the bright yellow of the wild roadside mullein species. Its height and airy, vertical form make it a classic cottage-garden and gravel-garden accent, working especially well toward the back of a border or threaded among lower perennials so its flower spikes read above the surrounding planting. Deadhead spent spikes to prolong bloom and expect this hybrid, like most garden verbascums, to be relatively short-lived, so divide or replace plants every few years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall; Cotswold Queen is one of the older English hybrid mulleins, bearing warm apricot-buff flowers with a violet eye.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage matters more than fertility for this rot-prone perennial. Cotswold Queen is a tall, long-established English hybrid mullein bearing dense spikes of warm apricot-buff flowers, each marked with a contrasting violet-purple eye, over gray-green, felted foliage. Its substantial height and warm coloring make it a striking vertical accent toward the back of a sunny border, pairing well with blues and purples that set off its buff tones. Like other hybrid mulleins it tends to be short-lived, so allow some self-sown seedlings to persist or divide and replant crowns every few years to keep the planting going.

common_name: Jackie in Pink Mullein (Dwarf Rose-Pink F1 Verbascum)

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface of lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall (do not cover — seeds need light); Jackie in Pink is a compact, seed-raised companion to the clonal 'Jackie' selection, bred for uniform rose-pink flowers on a dwarf plant.

directions: Sow seed on the soil surface in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since mullein rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Jackie in Pink produces compact spikes of rose-pink flowers with contrasting purple-mauve stamens over gray-green, felted foliage, staying dwarf and tidy enough for small borders, rock gardens, and containers where taller mulleins would look out of scale. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer; deadhead spent spikes to keep the planting tidy and encourage further bloom. Being seed-raised, individual plants can vary slightly in exact flower tone compared with vegetatively propagated selections.

common_name: Jackie in Purple Mullein (Dwarf Violet-Purple F1 Verbascum)

planting.note: Sow seed on the surface of lean, very well-drained soil in full sun in early spring or early fall (do not cover — seeds need light); Jackie in Purple is a compact, seed-raised companion to the clonal 'Jackie' selection, bred for uniform violet-purple flowers on a dwarf plant.

directions: Sow seed on the soil surface in lean, very well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since mullein rots readily in heavy, wet soil. Jackie in Purple produces compact spikes of rich violet-purple flowers with contrasting mauve stamens over gray-green, felted foliage, staying dwarf and tidy enough for small borders, rock gardens, and containers where taller mulleins would look out of scale. It flowers over a long season from late spring into summer; deadhead spent spikes to keep the planting tidy and encourage further bloom. Its deeper, richer color makes it a natural companion planted alongside Jackie in Pink for a two-tone dwarf mullein display.

planting.note: Establish from sprigs or plugs, not seed, since Tifton 68 is a sterile hybrid; plant once soil is consistently above 65°F. USDA-ARS breeder Glenn Burton released Tifton 68 in 1983 specifically for improved forage digestibility rather than raw yield.

directions: Establish Tifton 68 from sprigs or plugs in full sun into well-drained, fertile soil, since it is a sterile interspecific hybrid that sets no viable seed. Glenn Burton's USDA-ARS program at Tifton, Georgia released it in 1983 as a digestibility-focused advance over Coastal, and a decade later it was itself used as one of the two parents crossed to produce the even higher-quality Tifton 85, which has since largely replaced it in new plantings. It still persists in older hay and pasture stands valued for cattle weight gains that outperform Coastal on an equivalent-yield basis. Maintain a steady nitrogen fertility program and mow or graze regularly to keep the stand dense, since like other Tifton bermudagrasses it thins quickly under shade or neglect.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Bermudagrass for Forage
University of Georgia — Bermudagrass Forage Cultivar History
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Bermudagrass Cultivars for Texas

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Yellow Catuaí is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas bred Catuaí from a Mundo Novo x Caturra cross in 1949, and the resulting breeding population segregated into both red- and yellow-fruited forms, with the yellow color tracing back to a Bourbon ancestor's recessive gene. Catuaí Amarelo keeps the same compact, sturdy, early-bearing habit as its red sibling, but growers and cuppers often note a slightly sweeter, more delicate flavor along with a somewhat later, more even ripening window, since yellow cherries soften less obviously than red ones and are easier to leave on the branch a bit longer. Its dwarf stature and strong branch attachment keep it manageable in a large container and resistant to fruit drop in wind. Breeders have since used it as a parent of other compact yellow-fruited cultivars, including Obatã.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

common_name: Alampur Baneshan Mango (Historic Telangana Parent of Pickering)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun and well-drained soil; Alampur Baneshan is a historic Indian mango best suited to a warm, frost-free site with ample room to reach its mature size.

directions: Alampur Baneshan takes its name from the temple town of Alampur in present-day Telangana, where it has been grown for generations across the Deccan Plateau as one of South India's most widely planted commercial mango cultivars. The medium to large fruit ripens to a golden-yellow skin over fiberless, richly aromatic flesh with a well-balanced sweet-tart flavor prized for both fresh eating and juicing, and it was later carried to Florida as the parent of the compact dooryard cultivar Pickering. Like many Indian cultivars it tends toward alternate bearing and sets its heaviest crops after a dry, sunny bloom period that limits anthracnose. Shelter young trees from any frost and give the eventual canopy plenty of room, since established trees become large, long-lived specimens.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mango Growing in the Florida Home Landscape
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden — Mango Cultivar Notes

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Tafarikela is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Tafarikela is a heirloom Arabica landrace selected from wild and semi-wild coffee populations in Ethiopia, the species' center of origin, and long valued locally for its durable field tolerance rather than any single showcase trait. Indian coffee researchers crossed it with the Kent selection to breed S795, one of the most widely planted Arabica cultivars across South India and Southeast Asia, making Tafarikela an important but rarely cultivated-by-name ancestor behind that lineage. Rather than being sold as a distinct commercial cultivar, it survives mainly in Ethiopian farm gardens and germplasm collections maintained for coffee breeding. Grow it like other tall heirloom Arabica types, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade with steady warmth and moisture.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
